summary:
Dancing with the SARs — GERD / Lake Nigat is an interactive 3D Earth-observation web app built for NASA Space Apps 2026.   

It transforms real multi-mission radar imagery—four Sentinel-1 C-band VV scenes (2019–2025) and two NISAR L-band HH GCOV scenes (2026)—into a time-series map explorer of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) reservoir.   
To simplify complex radar interpretation, the platform combines a FastAPI backend, a MapLibre GL JS 3D terrain interface, live NASA Alaska Satellite Facility (ASF) catalog search, and a Gemini-powered Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) explainer grounded in a local SAR physics and hydrology knowledge base.   

Users can stack layers, blend acquisitions, inspect calibrated 12-day NISAR water-extent changes (+21.9 km² net change), and ask natural-language questions about why smooth open water appears dark via specular reflection while surrounding terrain scatters energy back.   

Because radar penetrates clouds day and night, this tool makes tracking rapid reservoir filling and short-term hydrological shifts accessible without specialized GIS software.   

While GERD serves as our proof-of-concept showcase due to hackathon compute and data-size constraints, the pipeline is region-agnostic and extendable to other Ethiopian ecosystems—such as tracking deforestation in the Bale Mountains or volcanic surface changes around Erta Ale in the Afar Triangle.
details:
Dancing with the SARs — GERD / Lake Nigat transforms real multi-mission Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) acquisitions over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) into an interactive 3D Earth-observation web explorer. It combines a six-date curated radar timeline—four Sentinel-1A C-band IW GRD VV scenes (2019–2025) and two NISAR L-band HH GCOV scenes (October–November 2026)—with live catalog search and an AI change explainer.

  • Data Processing Pipeline: Custom Python scripts ingest raw Sentinel-1 GeoTIFFs (reprojecting 210 Ground Control Points to EPSG:4326, converting digital numbers to decibels, and applying a 2%–98% contrast stretch) alongside full NISAR Level-2 GCOV HDF5 products (extracting 20 m frequency-A $\gamma^0$ linear power, converting to dB, and applying a common Otsu threshold of -14.053 dB to extract water masks and 12-day change metrics).
  • 3D Web Explorer: Users can stack multiple radar layers, adjust per-layer opacity, toggle NISAR water masks, animate time-series playback, and blend before/after acquisitions draped over 3D terrain.
  • Live NASA ASF Search: Queries NASA’s Alaska Satellite Facility (ASF) API across both Sentinel-1 (GRD_HD) and NISAR (GCOV) catalogs around any coordinate and date window, returning footprints, browse imagery, and download links.
  • Grounded AI Explainer (RAG): A Retrieval-Augmented Generation engine embeds a local Markdown knowledge base of SAR backscatter physics and GERD hydrology, retrieving relevant passages to answer user questions about why water appears dark (specular reflection) versus bright surrounding terrain and dam infrastructure.

Benefits & Intended Impact

Because radar waves penetrate cloud cover and operate day and night, SAR is ideal for monitoring tropical and seasonal regions like the Blue Nile basin where optical satellites are frequently blocked. However, raw SAR products are multi-gigabyte files requiring specialized GIS software and physics expertise to interpret.

This application bridges that gap by pre-processing heavy orbital datasets into lightweight web overlays and pairing visual comparison with an interactive physics explainer. Its intended impact is to democratize access to multi-mission radar hydrology—enabling students, researchers, policymakers, and regional stakeholders to visually track both multi-year reservoir filling and rapid 12-day NISAR repeat-pass surface water dynamics directly in a browser.

Tools, Languages, Hardware & Software Used

  • Languages: Python (62.8%), JavaScript (19.2%), CSS (10.2%), HTML (7.8%)
  • Backend & Geospatial Processing: FastAPI, Uvicorn, Pydantic, NumPy, Rasterio, h5py, Pillow, and asf_search / NASA ASF Search API
  • Frontend & 3D Mapping: MapLibre GL JS (v4.7.1), Esri World Imagery, AWS Terrain Tiles (Terrarium elevation), and vanilla HTML/CSS/JS with zero build-step overhead
  • AI & Retrieval: Google Gemini API (gemini-3.1-flash-lite for generation, gemini-embedding-001 for 3072-dimensional vector embeddings) with an in-memory NumPy cosine-similarity vector store
  • Satellite Data: ESA/Copernicus Sentinel-1A C-band GRD products and NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band GCOV HDF5 products accessed via NASA ASF

Creativity & Key Design Factors Considered

  • Dual-Mission Synergy: Rather than relying on a single sensor, the project bridges historical C-band monitoring (Sentinel-1, 2019–2025) with next-generation L-band 12-day repeat monitoring (NISAR, 2026), showing both long-term filling and short-term hydrological fluctuations (+21.9 km² net change, 0.870 Jaccard overlap).
  • Accessibility & Offline Resilience: Raw Sentinel-1 (~3.2 GB) and NISAR HDF5 (~3.5 GB) files are processed offline into lightweight RGBA PNGs so anyone can clone and run the app immediately without heavy downloads. Furthermore, the RAG engine includes an automatic lexical-retrieval and local metadata fallback so the platform remains functional even if external APIs or internet connections drop.
  • Scientific Transparency: The interface explicitly distinguishes between curated narrative estimates (Sentinel-1) and calibrated Otsu-thresholded measurements (NISAR), educating users on radar caveats such as radar shadow, speckle, and smooth terrain false positives.
  • Proof-of-Concept Scope & Generalizable Architecture: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD / Lake Nigat) serves as a focused demonstration case chosen due to hackathon time and local compute constraints when processing multi-gigabyte orbital SAR scenes (~3.2–3.5 GB per raw acquisition). Because the underlying pipeline—automated geocoding, dB backscatter calibration, Otsu thresholding, live NASA ASF catalog search, and RAG-grounded physics explanation—is completely region-agnostic, the exact same framework can be directly extended to monitor forest degradation and deforestation in the Bale Mountains (via volume-scattering loss in L-band/C-band) or volcanic deformation, lava flow emplacement, and surface changes around Erta Ale in the Afar Triangle.
